issues.legal_issue: De jure sovereignty over a territory is not transferred merely because a new power assumes its administration.
material_facts: The former ruler did not accede to the new Dominion, and the territory remained a separate state after the Dominion took over its administration.
A referendum later favoured accession, but no instrument of accession was executed.

The territory's administration was integrated with a neighbouring union of states under a supplementary covenant, after which that union's legislative and executive authority extended to the territory.
issues.conclusion: The Dominion did not acquire de jure sovereignty when it assumed administrative control; sovereignty passed only when the territory was integrated into the union of states.
issues.legal_principle: Acquisition of territory may be a continuous process, and the act of State terminates when the new sovereign assumes de jure sovereign powers; administrative control alone does not establish that transfer. The Court applied the reasoning in M/s. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax and State of Saurashtra v. Memon Haji Ismail Haji, and considered sections 5 and 6 of the Government of India Act, 1935, in determining whether the territory had become part of the Dominion.

predicates.territorial_sovereignty_transition_case: The proceeding requires a court to determine when sovereignty over a territory passed to a new sovereign.
predicates.administration_assumed_before_formal_int: The new power took over administration before a later formal act integrating the territory into its domain.
predicates.no_accession_agreement: The former territory did not accede to the new sovereign through an accession agreement.
predicates.separate_state_continued: The territory continued to be treated as a separate state after the new power assumed its administration.

issues.definition: When a sovereignty-transition case involves an administrative takeover before formal integration, and there was no accession agreement or the territory continued as a separate state, de jure sovereignty begins at formal integration.

issues.legal_issue: Orders affecting property made during an incomplete act of State cannot be challenged in municipal courts by the former state's inhabitants.
material_facts: The inhabitants or their predecessors held property under grants made by the former ruler.
An administrator acting for the new power cancelled or repudiated the grants and resumed the properties after taking over administration but before the territory's formal integration.
The affected holders brought civil suits seeking recovery of the properties, alleging that they had been taken without lawful authority.
issues.conclusion: The orders arose out of and during an act of State and were not justiciable in municipal courts; the suits were not maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: An act of State is an exercise of sovereign power against aliens and is not legally founded on municipal law; municipal tribunals cannot grant a remedy for actions arising from it, even if the action is arbitrary. The Court followed State of Saurashtra v. Memon Haji Ismail Haji and M/s. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and referred to Vajesinghji Joravarsingji v. Secretary of State for India. The administrator's orders, read in context, were acts of State rather than exercises of authority under law.

predicates.civil_property_suit_challenging_administ: A person brought a civil suit seeking relief from an administrator's order affecting property.
predicates.order_made_during_incomplete_sovereignty: The administrator made the order after the new power took over administration but before it completed its acquisition of sovereignty.
predicates.former_ruler_grant_not_recognized: The new sovereign did not recognize the property right claimed under a grant made by the former ruler.

issues.definition: A civil property suit challenging an administrator's order cannot obtain a municipal-court remedy when the order was made during an incomplete sovereignty transition and the new sovereign did not recognize the former ruler's grant.

issues.legal_issue: A court need not refer the timing of a sovereignty change to the government when the issue is a legal question and the relevant facts are clear.
material_facts: The parties disputed whether sovereignty changed when the new power assumed administration or only when the territory was later integrated.
The relevant political sequence was set out in an official government publication, and the Court found no uncertainty in the facts.
The dispute concerned whether the administrator's orders were justiciable, a question the Court considered for itself.
issues.conclusion: It was unnecessary to seek the Government of India's opinion on the timing of the sovereignty change.
issues.legal_principle: Although courts may seek government information about uncertain facts of State, the justiciability of a claim and the legal inference to be drawn from clear facts are matters for the court. The Court relied on the White Paper on Indian States as a clear account of the relevant political events and held that section 6 of the Extra-Provincial Jurisdiction Act, 1947 did not apply to these proceedings.

predicates.court_deciding_justiciability_of_adminis: A court is deciding whether a claim challenging an administrator's order may be heard by a municipal court.
predicates.sovereignty_timing_disputed: The parties disagree about when sovereignty over the territory passed to a new power.
predicates.relevant_facts_clear: The events relevant to the sovereignty change are not uncertain and are sufficiently established by the record.

issues.definition: When a court deciding justiciability faces a dispute about the timing of a sovereignty change but the relevant facts are clear, it need not refer the issue to the government.

issues.legal_issue: A former state's inhabitants can enforce pre-existing property rights against a new sovereign only if that sovereign recognizes those rights, and the property-rights protection does not itself create rights.
material_facts: The respondents claimed property under grants made by the former ruler.
The administrator's orders repudiated rather than recognized those grants.
The respondents argued that they could rely on the protection against deprivation of property without lawful authority after the new power assumed sovereignty.
issues.conclusion: In the separate opinion of Justices Sarkar and Mudholkar, the respondents could not enforce the unrecognized grants against the new sovereign, and the property-rights protection did not enlarge their rights; it protected only rights they already possessed against that sovereign.
issues.legal_principle: The separate opinion applied the rule that inhabitants of acquired territory may enforce against the new sovereign only rights that it has recognized, expressly or impliedly, or conferred by legislation. It relied on Cook v. Sprigg, Vajesinghji Joravarsingji v. Secretary of State for India, Secretary of State for India v. Bai Rajbai, M/s. Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, and Jagannath Agarwala v. State of Orissa. Section 299(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935 protected existing property rights but did not create or enlarge them.

rule.if: property_claim_against_new_sovereign and right_derived_from_former_ruler and not new_sovereign_recognized_right

predicates.property_claim_against_new_sovereign: A person claims a property right against a new sovereign in a municipal court.
predicates.right_derived_from_former_ruler: The claimed property right arose under a grant or other entitlement conferred by the former ruler.
predicates.new_sovereign_recognized_right: The new sovereign expressly or impliedly accepted the claimed right or conferred it by legislation.

issues.definition: A person claiming against a new sovereign under a former ruler's grant can enforce the right in a municipal court only if the new sovereign recognized it.
